[~accountid:712020:0c8dd65b-46d5-4dc0-b5bd-76209c1e8048] Hi! Njord got back with their advice. I’ve summarised it in the bullet-points below, in addition to the ODPO advice I already shared in my previous comment. In short, it confirms the position we already have.

*In short:*

* Consent is necessary, without consent this processing will be unlawful
** For RH, this may change in the future after EE has adapted the Directive (but not guaranteed that it will change)
* When asking for the consent, we must offer an alternative to the user (like we currently do with selfie checks)

----

*Further explanations:*

* For Bolt Drive, the *only* relevant legal basis grom GDPR art 9(2) would indeed be consent, as already brought out previously. The fact that consent (in the private sector) is the only possible legal basis for processing of special category data (such as biometrics) has been [emphasized by AKI as well|https://www.aki.ee/isikuandmed/kkk/moisted#yld-2], so consent is 100% a must-be and without it this processing is not lawful. In EE, there is no additional legislation re processing biometrics in the private sector.
* Re Ride-hailing (as it seems Product has plans to later expand this to Drivers as well), since Drivers are not employed under an employment contract, they would fall under the Directive (EU) 2024/2831 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 October 2024 on improving conditions in platform work. The deadline for adopting this directive is 2 December 2026, which means it is still *unclear what national legal provisions will be adopted by EE*. Until then, consent is the only suitable legal basis. 
** PS. In the future this may change once the Directive is adapted into national law (either EE or other member states, i.e. this would only be relevant for EU).
* Regarding the consent requirements: it is important to keep in mind that under GDPR art 7(4), there are the conditions for assessing whether consent is freely given. *As per Njord’s advice, it can be concluded that Bolt does not need biometrics to provide services and the consent can’t be conditional for Bolt’s services*.
* Currently, for the selfie check, we offer manual verification as an alternative and the same should be implemented for the fraud database as well. This means that Bolt has to offer an alternative to users when asking for consent to process and store their biometrics (to avoid the consent being conditional as in this case consent would not be freely given).

Hi [~accountid:712020:b25a56d4-6d1e-4c68-83ca-ebdda2617c3e] 

Splitting payments into multiple installments is something Bolt doesn’t currently do. If it’s something that is absolutely required then I could look into it. 

Customer debt collection is an issue that none of the teams have been working on. When the customer logs into the Bolt app they can see their balance. There should not be any additional notifications/emails to the customers regarding the negative bolt balance. 
There are two ways the customer can cover their debt. Either top up their balance or cover the negative balance with their next order. 

The negative balance is shared across all verticals. There is no such thing as “Drive balance” or “Delivery balance”. 
Fraud team decides which services the customers can use when they have a negative balance. It can depend on how much is the negative balance and which service is the customer trying to use. 

For example with small bolt balance debts we allow the customers to use the Ride Hailing service and to pay off their debt with their new order. 
Car rental service is usually the most restricted. 

Interestingly, the Bolt Balance debt also affects using the service in other currencies. For customers with a negative balance in PLN are also not able to place EUR orders until the PLN balance has been settled. 

Cheers, 
Marten

Discounts that were provided by Bolt to the Riders for the January accounted for the 182.20 EUR. Left is 110, right is 80 drum brake. For drum brake, the brake ring must be cast iron to ensure the braking performance，so 700g is almost impossible. 

Okai developed this iron ring 5 years ago， but it is said that this solution has not been used in recent years.

I have inquired with many brake manufacturers, and only Youmin has one case of Okai like this.

Here are some feedbacks from brake manufacturers：

* All manufacturers say that the iron ring of the drum brake is the responsibility of the motor manufacturer, not the drum brake manufacturer.
* They also do not recommend using additional iron rings. 
* The motor manufacturer also said that if a single iron ring is fixed with 6 screws, it is necessary to ensure the concentricity between the iron ring and the motor shaft, which is also a challenge. It is also recommended that it be made into a one-piece die-casting. 
* The iron ring is exposed outside, so rust prevention is also a problem, although rust prevention coating can be added.
* The drum brake cannot be as narrow as the expansion brake. So external iron rings cannot make the OLD smaller or even larger.

Hi[~accountid:5e4658b55a495e0c91a7a011] [~accountid:6215e9f275803500683497d5]  Even though we have made a decision, I think it is still necessary to share this information to you.

Kclamber visited our office today. Here is the info I  got from them.

ISIS shaft cost is more than 30RMB higher than JIS shaft because of the shaft process:

ISIS shaft process: Forging— CNC — 2 times heat treatment — Grind — gear hobbing — Surface treatment of zinc-nickel alloy

JIS shaft process: CNC — 1-time heat treatment — Grind — gear hobbing — ED

ISIS bearings are also bigger than JIS bearings, also a cost differences…

But in terms of riding performance, there is almost no difference. 

The main reason for the high cost of ISIS torque sensors is the processing cost of the shaft, bearings, cups, and the industry wants to create an image of high-end products and be more profitable. So ISIS is being developed into a high-end product in the industry. ISIS also has an advantage, which is that the crank will not fall off, unlike JIS, where the crank will loosen or even fall off when it is hit or intentionally damaged. But NB currently has a new solution that can prevent JIS cranks from falling off. The supplier will send me photos today or tomorrow.  CC: [~accountid:5f896ba2e357dd006e937e5b]

*Update (13.02) - NJORD shared its advice:*

*Original request to NJORD*

*Background:*
Problem 1. Users can have multiple Bolt profiles linked to the same email address. When they unsubscribe from one profile, other profiles remain active and continue receiving direct marketing communications. To fully unsubscribe, they must either:
* log into each profile and update preferences individually, or
* contact Bolt CS to request a global unsubscribe.
Problem 2. If a user unsubscribes via a link (i.e. email, SMS) rather than updating their Communication Preferences in the application, they are only unsubscribed from a specific category of marketing (e.g., "Promotions and Trips") for that channel (email, SMS). Other categories and channels still remain active. While the unsubscribe link informs users that they have unsubscribed from a category, it does not explicitly clarify that they may still be subscribed to other marketing channels. Full visibility and control are only available in the Bolts application Communication Preferences section.
We've identified the following risks under the GDPR:
# Lack of Transparency - users unsubscribing do not fully understand how their right to object is being executed - i.e. it does not affect other profiles.
# Violations of the Right to Object - the unsubscribe mechanism via links only applies to a category, not all marketing communications. There is a risk that regulators may determine that the right to object has not been respected.
*Scope of Assistance:*
*Please respond to the following:* would the setup per p. 1 and p. 2 be considered unlawful under Estonian law and case law? 

*NJORD's advice*

For the purpose of confirming/adding to the legal risks outlined in your e-mail, I’ve researched:
# The explanatory memorandum of the national law implementing the e-Privacy directive (Electronic Communications Act/ECA)
# Case law of the courts
# Case law/precepts of AKI
# Other material (noted below)
Both the case law of the application of the ECA as well as the application of GDPR, specifically the interpretation of GDPR art 5 (1) a), art 6 (1) a), art 7 and the right to object (art 21 (2), were analysed.
# *and 2.* Unfortunately there is nothing of relevance to report regarding the materials listed in points 1 and 2 
#  There is limited case law from AKI on the application of Electronic Communications Act in general, let alone on the granularity of objecting to data processing. The limited case law mainly dealt with controllers failing to fulfill the complainants’ requests to be deleted from the e-mail list.
There is one case ([no 2.1.6/21/15|https://www.aki.ee/sites/default/files/ettekirjutus-hoiatus_isikuandmete_kaitse_asjas_18.05.2021_nr_2.1.-6_21_15_tele2_eesti_aktsiaselts.pdf]) that dealt with the right to object specifically. In this case a telecommunications service provider (Tele 2) sent direct marketing messages to its customers. The customer had the opportunity, upon signing the agreement, to specify whether he/she wanted his/her contact information be used for the purposes of direct marketing. The customer didn’t agree to his/her contact information being used for direct marketing, but Tele 2 nonetheless sent him/her direct marketing messages. The messages contained a link, which allowed the customer to realize his/her right to object via using the self-service website.
AKI proposed that Tele 2 should implement an easier way for the data subject to exercise his/her right to object (either by having a direct link in the e-mail or by replying to the direct marketing e-mail directly). AKI’s opinion was that having the user log in to the self-service webpage was cumbersome. Tele 2 objected and referenced to the multiple ways of objecting to direct marketing, as well as referencing to other telecommunications companies’ practices.
AKI’s response to Tele 2’s response isn’t public and it is unknown if they addressed Tele 2’s objection. AKI terminated the case as the main issue (the complainant’s email address being listed in the marketing list) was resolved.
#  In the previously mentioned decision AKI referenced to it’s rather old [manual on the application of ECA|https://www.aki.ee/sites/default/files/dokumendid/elektrooniliste_kontaktandmete_kasutamine_otseturustuseks-uuendatud20.02.2015.pdf]. The manual does not provide any specific guidance on the possible approaches to the right to object to direct marketing, nor does AKI’s [general guidelines|https://www.aki.ee/sites/default/files/documents/2024-04/Isikuandmete%20t%C3%B6%C3%B6tleja%20%C3%BCldjuhend.pdf] on the application of GDPR provide any specific guidance.   
{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Conclusion:* As such, considering the limited case law available, no concrete conclusion on the unlawfulness of the mentioned setups may be drawn solely from Estonian law and case law alone. Additionally, the specific implementation of the e-Privacy directive into national law in the form of ECA (i.e. the wording of the law) and the case law do not point out to, or create, any specific additional risks that may arise from the two setups that you’ve mentioned.
{panel}

Based on the advice, Estonian law does not directly rule out the current Bolt’s direct marketing set up. Preparing to finalise the draft and share for the DPO alignment by Tuesday next week.

We received advice on US Privacy Notice from DLA. Here is a quick summary:

*Legal Requirement for a Privacy Notice*:

* There is no specific federal or DC law that mandates a privacy notice
* However, UDAP laws recommend businesses to be transparent and not misrepresent their data practices
* There are no specific provisions in the UDAP statutes or regulations that specify what information must be included in a privacy notice
* The FTC’s guidance for mobile apps (though outdated) suggests privacy notices should disclose:
** What information is collected
** How the information is used
** How the information is disclosed

*FTC Enforcement Risk*:

* The FTC considers it deceptive for companies to collect, use, or disclose personal data inconsistently with their published privacy notice.
* Enforcement risk arises from consumer complaints, media attention, or regulatory priorities.
* The FTC’s recent enforcement priorities were related to children’s data, health data, geolocation data and online browsing information.
* There is a potential risk of enforcement for failing to disclose how dashcam recordings are used.

*Next Steps:*

My high-level understanding of the Process (aided by an AI summary) is as follows. Let me know if I got anything wrong:

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
h3. *1. Initial Verification Steps*

When a driver lead (DL) reaches out claiming their email, phone number, or IBAN is already in use, the support agent follows these steps:

* *Access the Admin Panel*: Navigate to _Rides > Drivers > Edit_ to locate any existing driver accounts associated with the provided email or phone number.
* *Confirm Details with DL*: Ask the DL to verify the email or phone number they used for sign-up. If they confirm their credentials but still cannot register, further checks are required.

h3. *2. Duplicate Account Detection & Investigation*

If a duplicate account is found, the agent follows a structured investigation:

* *Check for Duplicate IBAN, Email, or Phone Number*:
** If a duplicate IBAN exists, proceed to IBAN verification.
** If a duplicate driver’s license is flagged, check the driver’s license database.
* *Verify the IBAN Ownership*:
** Compare IBAN owner details with the existing driver (ED) and DL.
** If payouts have been made to this IBAN, the account likely belongs to the IBAN owner.
** If no payouts exist, further investigation is required.
* *Cross-check Driver’s License Details*:
** Access the Local Regulatory Authority's verification portal.
** Compare the details of the driver’s license with the database.
** If DL’s license matches but ED’s doesn’t, potential identity theft is suspected.

h3. *3. Determining the Account Owner*

After verification, determine whether the account belongs to the ED or DL:

* *Account Likely Belongs to the ED If*:
** ED passes verification and IBAN matches.
** ED’s license is verified with the local authority.
* *Account Likely Belongs to the DL If*:
** ED fails verification or does not attempt it.
** DL’s license is valid per the regulatory authority, and IBAN is in DL’s name with no payouts.

h3. *4. Escalation & Resolution Steps*

Once verification is complete, the case is escalated based on findings:

* *If ED is the rightful owner*:
** Inform DL that an account already exists and advise them to log in.
** If their account is suspended, they cannot create a new one.
** Suggest contacting ED to update their details (email, phone, IBAN).
* *If DL is the rightful owner*:
** Escalate the case to the Local Operations (OPS) team.
** Suspend the ED’s account if fraud is detected and inform DL they can proceed with registration.
** Advise DL to contact the regulator to resolve document conflicts.

h3. *5. Handling Identity Theft Cases*

If identity theft is suspected, take additional precautions:

* *Suspend ED’s Account*: If verification fails, suspend the ED’s account due to fraud suspicion.
* *Request ED for Physical Verification*: If ED does not pass physical verification, suspend their account permanently.
* *Advise DL on Next Steps*:
** If DL’s details are valid, they can proceed with a new registration.
** If documentation conflicts exist, both parties should contact regulatory authorities.

h3. *6. Finalizing the Case & Updating Records*

* If DL is allowed to register, update their profile and remove duplicate information from the system.
* If ED refuses to cooperate, their account remains suspended, and DL proceeds with sign-up.
* Mark fraudulent accounts with notes to prevent further issues.
* In cases where ED is found guilty of fraud, escalate for profile deletion.

h3. *7. Communication with DL & ED*

* DL should be informed about the investigation status and that additional verification might take up to 3 business days.
* ED should be warned about fraudulent activity, and if they refuse cooperation, their account remains suspended.
* Final communication should include clear instructions for both parties on next steps based on findings.
{panel}

[~accountid:60f2a71843c956007065f2ad] please find response of our external lawyer below: 

“Indeed, the Competition Council report is drafted from the consumer's perspective and it deems that the differentiated tariff could be considered misleading, as it alters the price equilibrium principle which is advertised via the dynamic tariff. The report also assumes that the differentiated tariff is always applied in the best interest of drivers, since the platform's revenue is directly correlated with the driver's tariff.

Coming back to your question, the legal risk is higher in relation to lack of transparency towards the consumer, rather than the driver, for the reasons mentioned above. Fleets are professionals and they are bound by the T&Cs which do refer to the possibility of a variable base rate depending on market conditions. No less, the driver agrees to the tariff each time a ride is accepted, therefore it is not automatically applied by Bolt.

In B2B relations, reference could be made to the provisions of Law no. 11/1991, whereby it is considered an unfair competitive practice to exploit the superior negotiating position of an undertaking in relation to another undertaking with which it has or has had a commercial relationship, which causes material injury to the latter and is likely to affect competition in the market, by actions or inactions such as: unjustified refusal to supply or purchase goods or services, failure to comply with contractual terms concerning payment, supply or purchase, +*imposition of conditions which are unduly onerous or discriminatory in relation to the subject matter of the contract*+, or unjustified modification or termination of business relations with the partner undertaking. However this is merely theoretical, as it is difficult to assume the tariffs are unduly onerous and they apply the same to all drivers (for the same reasoning Art. 7 para. 3 let. d) in the P2B Regulation should not be reasonably applicable).”

In Dec 2024, we rolled out auto-fit for favourites: [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/CQL1E137B/p1734697468542299|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/CQL1E137B/p1734697468542299|smart-link] 

Problem: Home and Work locations cannot be adjusted from the eater app. Adjusting the pin for an order will not be remembered when the favorite location is selected again. This can lead to frustration when users have to manually adjust the pin again and again.

Solution: Retrieve the location of the latest order placed in a radius of 100m from the favorite location, and overwrite the favorite location’s coordinates with the previously adjusted coordinates. This only happens if that previous location was manually adjusted by the user, since the aim is to retrieve pin adjustments.

Last week (7th Feb 2025), we started A/B testing similar logic to current location: [https://taxify.slack.com/archives/CQL1E137B/p1739453689286739?thread_ts=1734697468.542299&cid=CQL1E137B|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/CQL1E137B/p1739453689286739?thread_ts=1734697468.542299&cid=CQL1E137B|smart-link] 

*Problem*
About 30% of app start-ups miss GPS, which prevents the app from automatically switching the delivery location to a historical location. Sometimes GPS is missing because the location is turned off, but other times the GPS is simply not available quick enough to trigger the automatic switch.
This doesn’t apply to *Current Location**_,_* which waits for GPS to load. However, *Current Location* often has an inaccurate address due to multiple factors such as building topology or flaky GPS.

*Solution* 

Since the feature that automatically switches the eater location to a historical one had [good results|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/GBM/pages/4777345947/Auto-fit+Auto-switch+eater+AB+test], to improve the relevance of *_Current Location,_* we will be replacing the *Current Location* with the latest historical location from a radius of 300m - if one exists.
Similarly to the start-up switch, this will only happen when for GPS accuracy < 50.

hey team! I found the leaflet that Glovo uses with the info on couriers from 16 years old. From the OPS perspective, we are ok with having individual entrepreneur couriers, but here comes lots of questions. 
1) we (I mean the ops team) won’t be able to help them with tax declarations/payments as Glovo does. probably we need to ask our accounting team/maybe outsource.
2) last time I asked (and I will check it again), our payment processing provider Wise cannot send money to individual entrepreneur bank accounts. 
Getting back to all the options regarding minor couriers, the most realistic is 

_First scenario - the employment of minors. Generally, minors can enter into employment agreements from 16 years old, and after that, we can engage them as employees of the fleet. At the same time, we would still need to require parental consent for accepting our T&Cs by such a minor._

Not sure we’d be able to cover tax payment for individual entrepreneur.

What is automatically provided to tax institutions?  For tax, we report VAT every month and invoices with this business client should be declared, is that what you refer to?  



{quote}The situation is that the Business admin requested to change the company name in the Business Portal on the 7th of January to UAB Divaks Food. * Not vice versa.  

So you can ask the client to provide the proof when the name change happened and when the VMI was notified.  If it is from January, invoice is correct.

How things look like today without any changes

Step 1. User has support widget open in inbox view
Step 2. Agent responds to the user
Step 3. Widget receives MQTT notification about a new message and triggers the refresh by invoking the endpoint through a callback provided to us by the portal
Step 4. Portal renders a unread count
Step 5. User opens the chat
Step 6. Webview uses RPC to notify widget that user has opened a support case and we should update unread cases
Step 7. Agent sends new message
Step 8. Both webview and widget will notify portal that there is a new message
Step 9. Too many requests

How it will look like with the changes
Step 2-7 remain the same
Step 8. Only widget will trigger the refresh
Step 9. Since mqtt arrives quickly, sometimes the refresh still returns the current case as unread (Which this PR is trying to fix)

The above didn't happen previously as webview and both triggered the call so by the time the second call finished, case had already been marked as read. But now with a single refresh, it doesn't always work.

Alternatively we could only rely on webview for refreshing when case is open and ignore the mqtt event on widget side, but unfortunately we can't see what url is open inside the iframe :/

{quote}Connect variables:

* _mysql-monitor_connect_interval_ – How frequently a connect check is performed, in milliseconds.
* _mysql-monitor_connect_timeout_ – Connection timeout in milliseconds. The current implementation rounds up this value to an integer number of seconds less or equal to the original interval, with 1 second as minimum. This lazy rounding is done because SSL connections are blocking calls.



Ping variables:

* _mysql-monitor_ping_interval_ – How frequently a ping check is performed, in milliseconds.
* _mysql-monitor_ping_timeout_ – Ping timeout in milliseconds.
* _mysql-monitor_ping_max_failures_ – If a host misses _mysql-monitor_ping_max_failures_ pings in a row, MySQL_Monitor informs MySQL_Hostgroup_Manager that the node is unreachable and that it should immediately kill all connections. It is important to note that in case a connection to the backend is not available, MySQL_Monitor will first try to connect in order to ping, therefore the time to detect that a node is down could be one of these two:
** _mysql-monitor_ping_max_failures_ * _mysql-monitor_connect_timeout_
** _mysql-monitor_ping_max_failures_ * _mysql-monitor_ping_timeout_{quote}



Current variables values are:

{noformat}+---------------------------------+----------------+
| variable_name                   | variable_value |
+---------------------------------+----------------+
| mysql-monitor_connect_interval  | 20000          | <- 20 seconds
| mysql-monitor_connect_timeout   | 200            | <- Rounded up to 1 second
| mysql-monitor_ping_interval     | 10000          | <- 10 seconds
| mysql-monitor_ping_max_failures | 6              |
| mysql-monitor_ping_timeout      | 1000           | <- 1 second
+---------------------------------+----------------+{noformat}

Meaning that ProxySQL takes at least 1 minute to consider a backend unreacheable.


Suggestion is to reduce to 40 seconds the time to consider a backend unreacheable, by:

* Reducing {{mysql-monitor_ping_max_failures = 4}} the ping is performed every 10 seconds up to 4 times.
* Set {{mysql-monitor_connect_timeout = 1000}} to its minimum, 1 second

Hey [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd], allow me to interject and provide more clarity!

By law, any fleet operator in Malta that has 5 vehicles or more, must have a public service garage (PSG). This is a permit that certifies the garage in which the cabs are parked, meets certain requirements.

When the law was passed, a grace period was allowed to give operators time to apply and get this permit. However, operators now have until the 18th of April to get their final approval. If not granted in time, the transport authorities will suspend their license to operate (until they have it).

Which means for us, commercially this could mean that come April 18th, a big chunk of our supply disappears overnight.

With that in mind, the purpose of collecting this document is so that we as Bolt, can start to assess our overall supply pool to understand (1) who already has the permit in place - no risk (2) those who have applied but are still pending approval - risk

To answer your specific questions:

* Are we mandated to collect - Maltese transport legislation does not stipulate (at least for now) what documentation platforms need to collect (in general I mean, not for this specifically)
* Information on the permit - yes it does have personal information but it should not contain information we do not already have to hand (fleet owner name, company details etc)
* Who will have access - assume this to be like any other document set
* How do we help operators understand - we can make direct reference to the legislation
* Deletion policy - feel free to guide us here, but once the April 18 deadline is hit, we can consider decommissioning the document set (on the assumption they stick to the current deadline it and don’t grant an extension)
* Will we be sharing this data to transport authorities etc - no, like I said, this is being done so we can assess the commercial risk



Here’s an article about the situation too: [https://www.maltatoday.com.mt/news/national/133441/crackdown_on_cab_operators_april_deadline_for_public_service_garages_is_do_or_die_|https://www.maltatoday.com.mt/news/national/133441/crackdown_on_cab_operators_april_deadline_for_public_service_garages_is_do_or_die_|smart-link]

After further analysis (on the sheet), it was determined that the following rule could be applied with the conditions:
{{and json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.flow') ='sign_in'}}

{{and json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.req_country') is null}}

{{and d.meta.country in ('ao','bd','ci','eg','gt','ke','my','tz','vn','zw')}}

{{having deviceUID_count<5 AND count(distinct user_id)>100}}



Full query:

{noformat}WITH sms_conformation_check AS (
    SELECT
        d.id,
        d.meta.user_id as user_id,
        d.created,
        d.meta.country AS phone_country,
        lower(json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.additional.ip_info.country_code')) ip_country,
    	json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.req_country') AS req_country,
        json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.phone_number') AS phone_number,           
        json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.method') AS Delivery_method,                   
        json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.client_ip') AS client_ip,
        json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.flow') flow,
        json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.user_handle.user_type') user_type,
        json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.app_verification_result.state') app_verification_result,
        --d.decision.decision,                                                                -- Decision (REJECT, ALLOWED, CHALLENGE, CHALLENGE_WEB)
     	json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.device_uid') device_uid,
     	json_format(json_extract(input, '$.additional.last_rides_finished_order.order_id')) as finished_order,
        rank() OVER (PARTITION BY json_extract_scalar(input, '$.data.phone_number'), DATE(d.created) ORDER BY d.created) AS rownum
    FROM 
        glue.archive_analytical.user_sms_confirmation_check AS d 
    WHERE 
        d.created_hour >= DATE_ADD('day', -31, NOW()) and created_hour  <= date_add('day',-1,now())
       --and json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.user_handle.user_type') in ('rider')
        and json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.flow') ='sign_in'
        and lower(d.decision.decision) not in ('reject')
        --and json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.app_verification_result.state') is null
        --and (json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.app_verification_result.state') in ('disabled','failed') or json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.app_verification_result.state') is null)
        and  d.meta.user_id is not null
        --and d.meta.country<>lower(json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.additional.ip_info.country_code'))
        --and lower(json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.additional.ip_info.country_code')) is null
        and json_extract_scalar(d.input, '$.data.req_country') is null
       --and json_format(json_extract(input, '$.additional.last_rides_finished_order')) is NULL
        and d.meta.country in ('ao','bd','ci','eg','gt','ke','my','tz','vn','zw')
),
fraud_user_log AS (
    SELECT
        id,
        u.created,
        phone,
        rank() OVER (PARTITION BY phone, DATE(created) ORDER BY created) AS rownum
    FROM 
        glue.ng_pii.fraud_user_sms_check_log AS u 
    WHERE 
        u.created >= DATE_ADD('day', -31, NOW()) and u.created  <= date_add('day',-1,now())
),
user_authorized AS (
select 
	 cast(created as date) created_date,
	 v.phone_number
	 from pii.user_authentication v
	 where
	 created_hour  >=  date_add('day',-31,now()) and created_hour  <= date_add('day',-1,now())
	  and name ='USER_AUTHORIZED'
	  and CAST(authorization_flow AS VARCHAR) = 'sign_in'
	 and phone_number is not null 
),
user_per_device AS (
    select
    	d.user_id as user_id,
    	d.phone_country as phone_country,
    	--count(DISTINCT d.finished_order) AS finished_order,
    	/*CASE 
        WHEN COUNT(finished_orders) = 0 THEN 'N/A' 
        ELSE CAST(COUNT(DISTINCT finished_orders) AS VARCHAR)
    END AS finished_orders,*/
        count(distinct d.device_uid) AS deviceUID_count,
  		count(DISTINCT d.phone_number) AS total_phone_numbers_count,
        COUNT(DISTINCT d.id) as total_otp_attempts_count,
        count(DISTINCT d.phone_number) FILTER (where not t.confirmed_at is NULL) phone_otp_verfied,
        COUNT(DISTINCT d.id) FILTER (WHERE not t.confirmed_at IS NULL) AS Attempts_otp_verified,
        count(DISTINCT d.phone_number) filter (where d.phone_number= ua.phone_number) successful_sign_in
   FROM 
        fraud_user_log AS u 
        LEFT JOIN sms_conformation_check d 
            ON d.phone_number = u.phone 
            AND CAST(u.created AS DATE) = CAST(d.created AS DATE) 
            AND u.rownum = d.rownum
        LEFT JOIN glue.ng_public.sms_conversion_tracking t 
            ON u.id = t.fraud_check_log_id
        LEFT JOIN user_authorized ua
    	ON  d.phone_number= ua.phone_number and CAST(d.created AS DATE)  = CAST(ua.created_date AS DATE) 
    GROUP BY d.user_id, d.phone_country
 --having count(distinct d.device_uid) > 4
)
SELECT 
--user_id,
phone_country,
 deviceUID_count,
 count(distinct user_id) as total_users, 
 sum(total_phone_numbers_count) total_phone_numbers_count,
 sum(phone_otp_verfied) phone_otp_verfied,
 /* --for cases where count(distinct user_id) = 0
 CASE WHEN sum(total_phone_numbers_count) > 0 THEN sum(phone_otp_verfied)/sum(total_phone_numbers_count*1.0)*100.0 ELSE 0 END AS Phones_OTP_conversion,
 sum(successful_sign_in) successful_sign_in,
 CASE WHEN sum(total_phone_numbers_count) > 0 THEN sum(successful_sign_in)/sum(total_phone_numbers_count*1.0)*100.0 ELSE 0 END AS Successful_signin_ratio, 
 sum(total_otp_attempts_count) total_otp_attempts_count,
 sum(Attempts_otp_verified) Attempts_otp_verified,
 CASE WHEN sum(total_otp_attempts_count) > 0 THEN sum(Attempts_otp_verified)/sum(total_otp_attempts_count*1.0)*100.0 ELSE 0 END AS Attempts_OTP_conversion
 */
 sum(phone_otp_verfied)/sum(total_phone_numbers_count*1.0)*100.0 Phones_OTP_conversion,
 sum(successful_sign_in) successful_sign_in,
 sum(successful_sign_in)/sum(total_phone_numbers_count*1.0)*100.0 Successful_signin_ratio, 
 sum(total_otp_attempts_count) total_otp_attempts_count,
 sum(Attempts_otp_verified)Attempts_otp_verified,
 sum(Attempts_otp_verified)/sum(total_otp_attempts_count*1.0) *100.0 Attempts_OTP_conversion
FROM user_per_device
GROUP BY 2,1
having count(distinct user_id) > 0 AND deviceUID_count<5 AND count(distinct user_id)>100
--ORDER BY deviceUID_count asc;
order by Attempts_OTP_conversion asc{noformat}

Normally, curfews apply to telemarketing (calls and SMS) only. Here are the key rules for telemarketing, including curfew times:

*Key rules to note when conducting telemarketing calls:*

* Telemarketers must register with the National Do Not Call List before making unsolicited calls, even if the calls being made are exempt.
* Telemarketers who make non-exempt telemarketing calls must both register with and subscribe to the National Do Not Call List. This subscription must be in effect for the period when the calls are being made and for the area codes for all numbers being called.
* Telemarketers must not make telemarketing calls to any number on the National Do Not Call List. Clients of lead generators (a company that is hired to make telemarketing calls) must adhere to this rule.
* The version of the National Do Not Call List being used by a telemarketer for compliance purposes must have been obtained no more than 31 days before initiating a telemarketing call.
* The National Do Not Call List cannot be used for any purpose other than complying with the _Telecommunications Act_ and the Unsolicited Telecommunication Rules.
* Telemarketers must maintain their own internal do not call list of numbers of consumers who have asked not to be called, even if these numbers are not on the National Do Not Call List.
* If a consumer asks a telemarketer not to call, the consumer’s phone number must be added to the telemarketer’s internal do not call list within 14 days and must remain on that list for 3 years and 14 days.
* Telemarketers must clearly identify themselves when calling.
* Telemarketers must respond to calls from consumers and must provide their contact information on request.
* *Calling curfews: Telemarketing calls can only be made between the hours of 9:00 a.m. and 9:30 p.m. on weekdays and between 10:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. on weekends.*

*Curfews should not apply to emails and push notifications. Let me know if this clarifies your concern.*

The difference comes from the driver (in this case driver fleet) VAT liability:
* if the driver/fleet is not VAT liable then the individual invoice is issued without VAT
* As Bolt is acting as reseller, and Bolt is VAT liable, the full ride price charged from the customer, will include VAT
* Customer can then reclaim all of the VAT charged on the aggregated invoice in their tax declaration.

For additional information or advice on how to word it neutrally (in a way that the customer will not feel like we overcharge them) please also consult with your regional Tax manager, Gerard can help you formulate an answer.

** *Account & Profile*: Account summary, favourite addresses (home and work)

** *Security*: Login history
* Attached file was deleted on the Bolt side. Recipient otherwise does not seem too concerned.

+*ANALYSIS*+

* We should fill out a personal data breach form for the DPO.
** May not be reportable, particularly if recipient does not open the file. The main concern is the photos of ID.
* We should ask CS at what exact time the file was deleted.
* CS should reach out to the user and ask them to: (1) not open the file; and (2) delete it on their side.
* CS should ensure that the actual DSAR is satisfied.

Hi [~accountid:60b0a48fd435380069b90208] , from a legal perspective, the existence of a CS ticket is irrelevant as long as we have justified reasons and grounds to block a courier and the courier is properly informed about the reason, the duration of the suspension, and their right to appeal. The CS ticket is merely an internal procedural and operational matter.

Please keep in mind that *one complaint is not enough*, as it could be subjective. There should be *multiple complaints* to justify blocking a courier - the more complaints we have, the stronger the argument that the courier’s service does not align with Bolt Food’s goals and user interests.

If you decide to block a courier, I *advise collecting actual feedback* from multiple providers, not just relying on selected reasons, as these could be biased and lack objectivity.

Thus, as a general rule: a negative courier rating should be substantiated by at least a few written complaints from clients or providers (not just selected reasons).

Summary of SPASS response to our email:

*Charging a penalty fee without warning in cases where vehicles have been incorrectly parked, where the amount charged will include the fine, towing fee, and daily fee, (€73, €79, or €82, depending on the year), to all fines meeting this criteria from 2023 onwards.*

*SPASS’s opinion is, overall, negative, based on the analysis below:*



+*_Pass-through to users without prior warning_*+

The collection of any fine should be *preceded by notification*:As Bolt has acknowledged on several occasions, the last user may not always be responsible for the poor location of the vehicle;Charging the fine without prior notice could lead to cases in which the user's account becomes overdrawn, which raises serious questions about the proportionality of the debit without prior notice;

* *_Application of the pass-through to older 2023 cases_*

This poses questions regarding the effectiveness of the contract, since fines are being charged for events from almost two years ago, which most likely will be considered disproportionate and not in good faith, especially if the user has not previously been informed retroactive charges - particularly if the T&C in effect at the time did not state this possibility, which results from a latter update.The imposition of penalties with such a time lag can undermine the user’s defense, further aggravating the imbalance between the parties and reinforcing the potentially abusive nature of the clause.The available case law in similar situations (charging fines without warning) concludes against the possibility of charging fines by debiting the user’s account without prior notice and without granting a period to exercise defense. Those decisions conclude that:

* Clauses allowing automatic charges without prior notice, or disproportionate penalties and payment of expenses without limits or without prior notice, are null and void, especially when there is no transparency regarding the amounts charged or the consequences for the consumer;
* In T&C’s, clauses must be clear and cannot grant the proponent excessive powers, such as automatic charging without prior notice;

+*Regarding Bolt’s questions:*+

+*_1 - No, it is not certain that you do not have to give prior notice to users._*+
While T&Cs may state that users will be charged penalties for breaches, consumer protection laws and case law states the importance of transparency and good faith, meaning users must be clearly informed about the breach and the penalty before any deduction is made.
The statement that you “_just have to let the riders know that they breached section 3.1 of the Driving Rules_” implies that prior notification is required. This ensures that users are aware of the breach and the impending charge.

In this regard, *SPASS recommends* sending a notification in the application or an email to users before deducting the penalty, informing them of the infringement, the applicable fine, the time of the deduction, and offering a reasonable time for them to exercise their defense, which minimizes the risk of complaints or legal challenges.

+*_2 - Yes, the likelihood of facing issues with the regulators is significant if you proceed with immediate collection of penalty fees without prior notice_*+, because:
·         Portuguese law prohibits abusive clauses and requires consumers to be treated fairly. Automatic deductions without prior notice are abusive, especially without prior warning.
·         Case law has consistently ruled against clauses that allow automatic deductions without transparency or the right to defense. This creates a strong precedent against such practices.

A possible compromise is to implement a short notice period combined with clear communication about the breach, consequences, and  right to contest. This reduces the risk of account deletions while complying with legal requirements. To minimize the risks of deletion you can offer payment plans or negotiating settlements, with the notification of the fine.

*_Therefore, regarding the likelihood of issues, SPASS labels them as high, if no prior notice is given, and moderate to low, if prior notice and a right to contest are provided._*

+*_3- Regarding the obligation to communicate to AMT changes/updates to our T&C’s_*+

Although the law does not explicitly state that operators must submit every change made to their T&Cs to the AMT, the AMT's understanding, as expressed in a public communication issued to other operator, makes it clear that operators are expected to notify the AMT of any future updates to their T&Cs, with identification the changes made.Non-compliance with the AMT’s requirements could result in fines or other penalties, and AMT may initiate injunctive actions to prohibit the use of non-compliant clauses. This could require Bolt to remove or amend clauses deemed unfair or abusive.



It is important to note that the *current advice just received from SPASS* differs from the initial analysis of the *pass-through feature* for several reasons:

* The *previous analysis was conducted on an urgent basis* and did not fully assess the consumer law risks related to collecting payments without providing users with reasonable notice.
* The *original analysis took place two years ago*, whereas we are now considering applying *penalties to 2023 cases*.
* Over the past two years, we have faced *increased regulatory scrutiny*, with *multiple inquiries from AMT, consumer regulators, and privacy authorities*.
* Many *Ride users have filed complaints with AMT*, and *MM users could do the same*. In such a scenario, it is almost certain that we would be asked to remove the penalty clauses from our T&Cs (_best case_), or we could face fines or even the risk of losing our license (_worst case_) - given that the T&Cs containing the penalty clauses have not been communicated to AMT.

These factors have led to the adoption of a *more cautious and conservative approach, and we recommend to:*

* *Start recovering fines using the 'fines pass through' feature, configured to give 14 days notice.* If we observe poor collection rates or high CS tickets, we can better assess the risk associated with a lower (e.g. 7 days) or no notice period for collections.
* *For fines issued +3 months ago, action collections for a limited volume (rather than the whole amount).* Again we should observe collection rates and CS tickets and scale up recoveries if signals look good.

*If immediate collection is the management decision*, we request you to acknowledge i) the *risk that complaints to the PT Consumer Protection as well as Transport Regulator are very possible*, in particular for historical fines and ii) in the event of an investigation, *it may not be limited to fines handling in MM and may extend to other customer interactions and/or Bolts ride-hailing and delivery verticals in the market.*

Hey [~accountid:60b0a48fd435380069b90208] !

Apologies for the delay in getting back to you on this ticket.

Unfortunately, I cannot approve the decision to stop checking individual activity certificates. While there is no specific law explicitly requiring us to do so, this obligation arises from the overall holistic set of duties and responsibilities of a responsible and diligent merchant. The company must conduct basic due diligence to ensure it is doing business with or offering its services to compliant parties. Therefore, a basic level of partners' due diligence is essential.

If we allow unrestricted access to our platform for anyone claiming to be registered with tax authorities, there is a risk that, in the event of a tax evasion case involving a courier or a group of couriers (who are not registered and therefore do not pay taxes), a claim could be made against us for failing to perform basic partner due diligence and thus we become involved in tax evasion cases. This could lead to allegations that we facilitated tax evasion by allowing non-compliant parties to use our platform. Therefore, we need to maintain basic measures to ensure a minimum level of compliance among our supply partners.

If checking registration certificates is too resource-intensive, I suggest exploring the following options:

# *Integration with tax authorities* – we could discuss the possibility of integrating our courier database with the VMI database. This way, we would receive notifications if any of our registered couriers are missing from the VMI system, or such couriers could be automatically suspended from our platform. We are having similar discussions with LV transportation authorities for drivers, so this should be doable also in LT - needs to be discussed with Jaagup then. 
# *Selective certificate checks* – If integration is not an option, we should require couriers to upload a copy of their registration certificate upon onboarding. Are they required to do this currently, or do they only submit their taxpayer number Further, we should conduct selective checks from time to time. This means we will retain the verification process but on a smaller scale and a selective basis. While this approach will reduce the workload, some unregistered couriers may still slip through. However, it allows us to maintain a basic level of due diligence in a more limited capacity due to resource constraints - certainly better than nothing. Let me know your thoughts.

I appreciate CityBee has the same process in place based on their public information, it’s not transparent to us how they conduct such verifications and their logic, what their risk tolerance is and what legal basis and exception they use.

*After the review of our process described by the team in the DPIA, I have the following thoughts:*

{panel:bgColor=#fffae6}
*Disproportionality of the measures to the actual purpose*
{panel}

While I truly appreciate the efforts and the goal of the team, *the measure of storing for a long period and comparing the facial measurements afterwards seem to be excessive and disproportionate to the goal* of preventing duplicate accounts (_as just a clearance process of not having many accounts_) and preventing fraudulent users to use our platform (_eg blocked drivers getting back to the platform_). 

I recognise that the *facial measurements are one of the characteristics* that *do not change over time*, using special categories of data that are highly strict to the security and privacy requirements (such as of properly storing, encrypting, ensuring access controls and proper lawful re-use of this data) is not a best deal. Bolt is not a regulated company like fintech, bank, credit or crypto platforms, nor a health company. *Introducing such a measure of fraud prevention can undermine the actual purpose limitation of this project and be recognised irrelevant to the risks posed.* 

Please note that SAs and EDPB are quite strict to using appropriate verification measures to the risk being caused.

{panel:bgColor=#e3fcef}
*Reconsidering the measures appropriate to the goal*
{panel}

As mentioned, while I recognise and agree facial measurements are one of the most static things in this world, the team can *consider other alternatives* to eliminate risks in the DPIA and ensure smooth process (see explanations in parts below). For example:

* Our verification systems are able not to only extract facial measurements from a photo/document, but also to extract DATA from the document.
* It means that we can consider to match name, surname and date of birth for this process instead of the facial measurements.
* As drivers at Bolt Drive provide their driving licenses to us, their name and surname on the later document will unlikely change over time, unless they replace their passport and change name/surname.
* As this is a document linked to the government-issued ID (names and surnames should match), this measure of verification seems to be more appropriate and helpful to achieve our goal.
* It means when a driver uploads a driving license, our system will extract name/surname/DOB from this license and compare it to other extracted names/surnames/DOBs in the database from other driving licenses.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Benefits of reconsidering the measure* 
{panel}

As noted by Eliise in her assessment and by Lev in the DPIA, 

* We would need I*NFORMED consent* (that is strict in particular with special categories of data) for reusing the facial measurements for later comparison and for storing this data longer than necessary for the initial goal.
* Consent is not the best choice (in our case we have no choice even). *If the person rejects this process after the INFORMED consent we will give and specify the purpose such as fraud prevention, we will not be able to conduct any of the checks without consent.*{color:#bf2600} It means that we will have small % of users going though such verifications.  {color}
* The end goal of this project will not be achieved with this setup when we ensure compliance with the GDPR. 
* If we reconsider the approach as specified above or similar to this, we will exclude any special categories of data from the process, eg we can rely on a legitimate interest. It means we do not need a consent of the user to conduct this check and we will have big % of users going through the verifications.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*Downsides and legal basis if we proceed with facial measurements*
{panel}

I agree that they only exception we can apply under Art 9 is an explicit consent. However, we will need two consents:

* Before the driver uploads any docs/photos to us, *we need to ask a consent for biometric verification.* Our standard process we leverage now.
* However, we would also need another *consent for reusing these measurements for another purpose* and, consequently, extensive storage of such measurements for later comparison.
* It means a user needs to be *provided with 2 consents before they start the verification for ordering a ride.* 
** This will provide *bad experience to the user* (users are usually in rush to be verified and take a ride) and can be considered a *dark pattern* given we provide too much consents when we anticipate users are in rush, eg they will not read and just consent.

h3. Testing to determine possible solutions

Conditions - to create/simulate a “dead scooter”, the main battery was discharged with an electronic load so that output was 0V. IOT backup battery was discharged.

h4. Test procedure

* Create a “dead” scooter with all working components connected & completely discharged battery inside.
* Using a DC PSU, supply different voltages from 0V upwards with 0.5V increments via vehicle charging port.
* Determine voltage where controller was able to provide power to the lock and IOT in a stable way, without starting to charge the battery (avoid large current).

h4. Results

* :red_cross: At 0 - 17.5 V, there was no response from the vehicle whatsoever, current consumption on the PSU was 0A.
** This voltage range can not be used for powering the hatch lock & IOT. 
* ⚠️ At ~18.0 - 30.0 V, the controller supplied power to the controller, hatch lock init was successful. The IOT started booting, but blanked out in ~10 second period. This loop continued in each 0.5V increment in that range, IOT was not able to boot up correctly.
** This voltage range can not be used for powering the hatch lock & IOT. 
* (/) At 30.5 - 31.5 V, the controller supplied power to the controller, hatch lock init was successful. IOT started booting and successfully booted and stayed on. Tested stable IOT behavior for 10min. Responsive to unlock commands, max. current peaked at ~17 mA, making the max power consumed 5.27W
** This voltage range *can be used* for powering the hatch lock & IOT. 
* (i)  At 32.0 - 33.0 V, the controller supplied power to the controller, hatch lock init was successful. IOT started booting and successfully booted and stayed on.  Vehicle was formerly in POWER_ON mode, at 32V+ the controller opened the light output, which did not happen at the previous known-good range. That increased the max. current to 25mA. This is not
** This voltage range *can be used* for powering the hatch lock & IOT.

h4. Conclusion

The wake up tool needs to supply 30.5 - 31.5 V output. To be safe, output current should be no less than 0.5A to avoid peaks in different situations.

There are no household/regular WH equipment that I could think, of which could supply such high & controlled voltage.

The solution could be a DC-DC regulator, i.e. *USB interface (5V) -> DC-DC converter → fixed 31.0 ± 0.5 V DC output*. USB interface would be good as most modern power banks can deliver 5V 2A (10W) without communication to the consumer. This would also help keep the tool only as a passive component.

Another option would be to adapt the same idea as before, but instead USB interface, use some familiar Makita battery connectors to use drill batteries.

TWS reply:

*Bolt:* Could you please clarify how the battery handles a failed firmware update? Ideally, if an update fails, the battery should automatically roll back to the previous firmware version. Does your BMS support this functionality?

*TWS:* BMS is in boot mode. à Firmware update failure à  No communication for 3 minutes à  Boot will roll back the latest backup version firmware to MCU.  à if rolling back the latest firmware version fails (3 attempts) à Boot will roll back the previously backup the factory firmware version to MCU.

We tested with two batteries, and when the battery update failed, the battery automatically rolled back to the previous firmware version or factory firmware version.

Can you share with us more details about the inability to roll back firmware after a failed battery update? How many batteries to update? How many batteries have this phenomenon? And so on. We want to prepare some more battery tests to try and replicate the anomaly.

Can you share with us the logic of IOT updating BMS firmware?

For example, BMS firmware is sent to IOT over 4G networks; IOT receives the complete BMS firmware validation OK and saves it to IOT flash or RAM. (BMS firmware is generally updated in the early morning) IOT monitors that the scooter is not in use and begins to update the BMS firmware. IOT determines that the BMS firmware is updated successfully, then the scooter works normally. If the BMS firmware fails to be updated, disconnect the communication for a period of time, wait for the BMS to roll back the firmware, and try to update the BMS firmware again.

 

*Bolt:* Also, I want to point out that the binary file size is multiple times larger compared to other suppliers. As a result, the firmware update process takes 2–3 times longer. Please optimize your code to reduce the file size by at least half.

*TWS:* At present, the D1 development platform contains large content (some checks and event records of the TWS platform, etc.), and the generated upgrade documents are also larger. The project function has been developed and perfected. It's not easy to make big optimization. Too much optimization, fear of other unknown risks.

Your main concern right now is. If IOT fails to update the BMS firmware, BMS will not automatically roll back to the previous firmware version. When BMS disables output, the battery and scooter cannot be found. Is that right?

Please accept our apologies for the extended delay in addressing this matter. The implementation of new regulations caused this process to be deprioritized, but we are now prepared to proceed. We appreciate your previous contributions and wish to establish a clear, documented, and legally/privacy-compliant process.

Our objective is to create a well-defined procedure for requesting limited-scope (5-year standard) administrative offense information from [http://epolicija.lt|http://epolicija.lt|smart-link] . This information will be used to assess driver suitability for our platform.

*Instances for Requesting Administrative Offense Documents:*

We will request this documentation only under the following specific circumstances:

# *Third-Party Information Regarding Criminal Past:* A third party informs us of a driver's alleged criminal past, and we possess corroborating evidence from reputable media sources. While reputation risk is a consideration, we recognize the importance of equal opportunity. The administrative offense document will provide necessary ground for any decision not to onboard a driver in these cases.
# *Information from Past Records:* We have existing records (from periods when we collected background documents) that raise concerns about a driver's suitability. If these older documents contain potentially disqualifying information, we may request a more recently issued administrative offense document for clarification if the driver is registering on our platform again.
# *Reports of Driver Intoxication:* We receive a report stating that a driver was intoxicated while operating a vehicle. This report will trigger a request for administrative offense information only if it is a recurring report for the same driver or if it is a first-time report accompanied by other supporting indicators, such as:
#* Driving speed
#* Proof sent from rider
#* Bad ratings in the same timeframe
#* Suspicious rider comments

*Key Points of Concern in Administrative Offense Documents:*

We will be particularly concerned with the following information found in administrative offense documents:

* Any information on alcohol use (publicly, driving).
* Violence (publicly, at home).
* Any illegal substance-related records.
* Repetitive speeding/unsafe driving complaints.

To move forward with establishing this as an official local process, we need to determine the specific operational steps required. [~accountid:712020:a7a7d4bc-10ca-44a0-a22e-fa8752330abd]  please advise on the necessary actions from an operational perspective to finalize and implement this process.

Answering your questions: 

* *Services:*
** Bolt Ops OU will continue to offer app/platform services (the same as now). This will apply at least until is potentially implemented in 2026 and, we can consider full localization.
** Drivers/fleets will continue to provide transportation services to riders (the same as now).
* *Contracts:*
** Drivers, fleets, and riders will have T&Cs with Bolt Ops OU. The payment agent section may need to be updated, as rider payments should go to the financial company City24  in the new setup.
** Large fleets may need contracts with City24 due to financial monitoring requirements as their turnover can be high and fin. companies should have KYC/contracts in such cases.
** Bolt Ops OU can’t have an ordinary contract with City24. I would also like to address the question of [~accountid:60b5deeb5fa6f1006f994b75] there. Since City24 (and other Ukrainian financial companies) cannot sign a standard contract with a non-resident, hybrid solutions are proposed by them. These may include a 3-party contract - Bolt Ops OU, City24 and a local intermediary entity (let’s name it SPV) - or a contract with a local legal entity acting on behalf of Bolt Ops OU. This local SPV could be related to City24 or Bolt, depending on the agreed-upon risks, structure, and commercial conditions.  The reason we need it - 1) City24 cannot contract directly with non-residents. 2) Bolt perceives risk in utilizing the local setup, this may change following DAC7 implementation.
** Bolt Ops OU and the local SPV would need a commission or agency agreement (or another applicable contract).
* *Invoicing:*
** Drivers/fleets will continue to issue invoices for transportation services to riders (the same as now).
** Bolt Ops OU will continue to issue invoices for commission fees to drivers/fleets (the same as now).
* *Payments:*
** City24 will manage payments, receive money from riders, hold funds, split the balance for drivers/fleets, and make payouts to them.
** Bolt's commission can be paid from City24 to a local Bolt entity, the SPV, or held by City24 for a period.
** Bolt will NOT make payouts to drivers/fleets mitigating the withholding tax risk. 

I would be happy to answer other questions if you have any.

Hey Justus! Thank you for the follow-up:- 


* *Just to be sure, this is for Cleaning Fees only, correct?*
** Yes, this is specifically for the Cleaning Fees that were incurred by the driver due to “User Made Mess” ATI.
* *How does it work? What is an ETR? Does every ETR come with a PIN?*
** An *ETR* is an Electronic Tax Register—a type of cash register that records all transactions between a buyer and a supplier.
** Here’s how it works: The driver provides an ETR (Electronic Tax Register) receipt as proof of the cleaning expense. We require this because, in the past, we received fake receipts before transitioning to the KRA (Kenya Revenue Authority) receipts. Most ETR receipts are legitimate as they’re issued by tax-compliant businesses.
** *Yes,* every ETR comes with a PIN. The PIN is linked to the business issuing the receipt. We use the KRA Pin Checker to verify these PINs, and since it’s a government tool, it’s reliable and trustworthy for confirming the validity of the PIN.
* *Why are we adding the PIN check to the process?*
** We’re adding this step to improve the compensation process. Some drivers have been submitting false ETR receipts with invalid PINs to manipulate the system and claim compensations unfairly (As per the samples shared above). By verifying the PIN, we can confirm if the business that issued the ETR is VAT-approved and legitimate. This helps us ensure that only genuine claims are processed.

*Analyzing modelling period change*

Checking whether period per se could make substantial difference (this is main Avishek’s concern). 

For this, I did the following:

* run the same model as were run in Q3 (from the Q3 notebooks folder, [here|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/1666917710951523?o=3829506390716583#command/1666917710951524])
* only change the “post” period (additional Q4 data)
* change both “pre” and “post” parts (so that the period is similar to what we have in our actual models for Q4)

Note that 

* priors were not changed at all.
* results were compared to the mean of Q3’s vmax, not the upper bound

Results are collected [here|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1cL6Ur8uJh5oA-DFlrSGYpGsNPc18yik81vORRcSj6Pw/edit?pli=1&gid=2134207199#gid=2134207199] in analyzing_big_drops in columns F, I, K.

* One can see that in France, Germany and Sweden, changing the period does not lead to significant changes in resulting vmax's. 
** The changes for these markets will be analyzed in further comments
* In UK and Poland some (not all) channels changed their coefficients



*Analyzing changes in countries where period per se changed the coefficients.*

Analysis requires that we understand, at which exactly date the coefficient changes. 

We are OK with the situation, where:

* the channel changes after some intervention has happened (i.e. we’ve changed the cost, the model changes the coefficient based on observed results)
* the change happens gradually (not just drops during one week). This would be a sign of model unrobustness.



So for UK and Poland we trained the models that would incrementally add one week from Q3 to Q4 (priors are same) to check the dynamics of the change:

* This was done in [[Automating Periods]|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/2934471359380040?o=3829506390716583#command/2934471359380041] folder, results were collected in {{dev_martech_spark.martech_6423_vmax_dynamic}} and analysed in [this|https://bolt-datascience.cloud.databricks.com/editor/notebooks/2934471359373645?o=3829506390716583#command/8478685154296235] notebook.
* The findings are:
** Changes do not happen immediately (over the course of 3-4 weeks)
** Changes happen only when costs are changed (i.e. models obtain additional signal)
** Coefficients are stable before and after the ad change (this confirms that the models are generally robust)

Hi! [~accountid:5bb1cc64c9dad04734ea835a] [~accountid:6149a0e9ba1b34006ab04897] [~accountid:712020:53555a79-b384-46b1-8f21-2b13cb2c655a]  (sorry for the long comment) leaving here for the record Amilon argument on the license for this activity and my opinion on it. 

Under the agreement they shared with us, they are the distributor of the “gift cards” Bolt issues. This activity according to them (the gift card as a payment instrument) is not regulated, under the following argument: 

_“it should be noted that gift cards, even if constituting a payment instrument, shall not be considered as a “payment service” according to art. 3 (k) of the “_[+_Directive (EU) 2015/2366_+|https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/PDF/?uri=CELEX:32015L2366] _(“PSD2”), thus resulting in the inapplicability of the PSD2 (and the national implementing legislation consequently)._

_Consistently, also Article 1(4) of Electronic Money Directive 2009/110/EC provides that its rules do not apply to monetary value stored on instruments excluded under Article 3(k) of PSD2._

_In light of the above, entities that issue gift cards – which fall within the scope of the so-called “limited network exclusion” - are not required to obtain licences._

_In any case, it should be considered that_ *_Amilon is merely a distributor, rather than the issuer_*_. That said, while there may indeed be heterogeneous applications of EU law across different jurisdictions, we are not aware of any requirement to obtain a licence.“_

According to their answer, these “gift cards“ offered under this agreement, are not considered to be a financial instrument, as in this agreement it appears to be a closed-loop card. The company cites *Article 3(k) of PSD2*, which excludes certain instruments from being classified as payment services, including those used within a *"limited network."* If the gift cards are only redeemable at a specific retailer or within a clearly limited group of merchants, they *likely* fall under the "limited network exemption," meaning PSD2 wouldn't apply. 

Based on this, it seems like gift cards, depending on their structure and usage, may or may not be considered financial instruments under [PSD2. |http://PSD2.In]In their agreement, the definition of “gift card” suggests it functions more as a voucher for goods and services rather than a financial instrument used for payments under PSD2.  

*Note* that the funds *should be paid to Bolt once the gift card has been redeemed*. Amilon needs to hold the funds of the gift cards sold and only pay Bolt those amounts from redeemed gift cards. They will be holding funds on behalf of others under their own risk.

* What about refunds? are the cards refundable before they are used? where does the customer claims the refund?
